extracted.intended_audience: aspiring novelists, fiction writers, and critics studying narrative technique
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on selecting and applying narrative methods (dramatic/scenic vs. pictorial/narratorial) in novels, including when to dramatize inner life, when to use a narrator, and how scope and subject determine method.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dramatization of inner life (showing, not telling)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use dramatization — let the remote manifestations of an inner agitation enact themselves so the reader perceives the mind’s struggles without direct exposition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The method enables an onlooker to 'see round the object' and gives 'solidity, weight, a third dimension' to a character's case (example: Milly). Rather than underlining words about a state, let the surface disturbances, gestures, looks, and interactions reveal the inner force; enact the remotest manifestations to represent strength, bulk, and range in a harassed existence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make use of 'looks and gestures' as objective signs of thought
rubrics_metrics.description: Express thinking and feeling through tell-tale gestures and speaking looks so that thought is 'enacted' rather than narrated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Thought can be dramatized because it has observable signs; use these signs so the process of thinking and feeling is 'exposed objectively to the view of the reader' (Strether-style books). This produces a 'silent drama' that plays before the reader, often more effective than explicit interior narration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use a narrator only when he contributes definite value
rubrics_metrics.description: If the presence of a seer/recorder (narrator) does not add materially to the effect, it is better to dispense with him and give the reader a direct view.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The narrator is valuable when he is himself a contribution to the effect (economy, picture-making, foreshortening, or where the subject requires reflection). But if he exists merely for the author's convenience, he may embarrass or weaken the story; prefer direct dramatic presentation when appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Match method to the scope/amount of the subject
rubrics_metrics.description: Let the reach and quantity of the subject determine whether the dramatic method will suffice or whether the narrator/chronicler is required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A large, extensive, panoramic subject (crowds, breadth in time/space) 'exceeds the capacity of the straight and dramatic method' and calls for a narrator (examples: Thackeray's chronicles, Esmond, The Virginians). Small, compact situations are better served by scenic/dramatic presentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dramatic subject = action-centered storytelling
rubrics_metrics.description: When the core of the story is a question of action — 'What will these people do?' — the subject is dramatic and should be shown through behaviour and scenes rather than interior exposition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In action-focused books (example: The Awkward Age and Nanda's case), the issue lies in behaviour and visible acts; action alone can cover motives and sentiments if carefully managed by the author. Such subjects often require little or no narrator.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pictorial/undramatic subjects may require narrator or indirect treatment
rubrics_metrics.description: When emphasis falls on gradual changes of mind, character, or inward reverberation rather than outward action, a pictorial or reflective method (narration, summary, or indirect presentation) may be more expressive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Books like Madame Bovary or The Ambassadors have subjects 'undramatic in their matter'—their power lies in inner change and pictured impressions. They might be scenically treated, but dramatization may not make the most of such subjects; the narrator can project a particular point of view for clarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistency of method when choosing a dramatic approach
rubrics_metrics.description: If you adopt the dramatic (scenic) method throughout, maintain strict consistency: submit to the constraints of the playwright to secure compactness and direct force.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Awkward Age is cited as a novel that never deviates from pure drama: no omniscience, no retrospection, everything immediate and particular. This yields a 'complete' and 'true to itself' effect but is difficult to sustain; ensure scenes, dialogue, and stage-like directions carry all necessary information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Narrator as principle of economy and picture-making
rubrics_metrics.description: When the subject requires summary, panoramic survey, or a foreshortened account, the narrator is a valuable device for economy and for framing the picture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many large or panoramic stories 'postulate the story-teller' who draws back for a general view; the narrator can represent the story compactly and contribute positively to effect where direct drama would be impractical.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid over-narration that forces vivid drama into summary
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not let a voluble narrator 'embarrass' a matter of vivid drama by converting it into pure narration; unnecessary commentary can weaken immediate scenes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critique the convenience-driven narrator who 'comes forward' without helping the story; if a matter is dramatic, allow it to unfold unaided rather than remarking on it at length—this preserves immediacy and impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure essential background/civilization is rendered when it matters
rubrics_metrics.description: If a story's issue depends on a particular social setting or background, that background must be clearly shown; strict scenic method may fail to make a singular background evident.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Nanda's little world is an example: her setting is 'important' to her case and may need pictorial presentation rather than pure immediate scenes. Choose method(s) that make essential background and its odd quality visible and known.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be pragmatic about mixing methods; pure rigor is difficult
rubrics_metrics.description: While pure dramatic method can be powerful, treating a subject with such rigour is difficult; novelists commonly mix omniscient narration and scenic presentation to practical effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It is often simpler to 'use his omniscience' to explain actions than to make characters act entirely self-explanatorily. Critics may neglect the theory, and authors routinely blend methods for clarity, background, and effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Let scenes embody appeals and implications rather than explicit statements
rubrics_metrics.description: Design scenes so that appeals, moral implications, and turning-points 'hang in the air' and are embodied in the room, light, movement, and speech rather than delivered as statements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Susan-and-Densher scene demonstrates how the falling light, uneasy movements, broken phrases, and surroundings contribute to an appeal without a direct announcement. Aim for scenes that make meanings 'actual and palpable.'
